parts.text: Why each removal. Blowout preventer seals and wellhead O-rings are API 6A / 16A parts — qualification Margo does not hold and lists as a roadmap item on its own oil & gas page. Syringe plunger tips and peristaltic pump tubing are device-contact components requiring ISO 13485; /industries/medical-devices states plainly that Margo does not hold it. Conveyor belt scrapers, crusher wear pads and slurry pump seals are wear consumables, and the mining page’s entire positioning is precision-moulded-OEM-supplier rather than wear-parts reseller — the hub card contradicts the page it links to. Tank linings and impeller wear rings are fabricated or machined items, not moulded parts. Refrigerant seals need a compound rated for the specific refrigerant, which is a per-programme question, not a catalogue claim.

Every replacement part is named in Margo’s own company profile or catalogue. Descriptions stay at 10–14 words, matching the live card height. Automotive gains the four parts the profile actually names, which are more specific and more persuasive than the generic three they replace.
parts.lead: Every replacement part is named in Margo’s own company profile or catalogue.

notes: Nine internal links out, anchor text “Rubber components for {industry}” rather than nine identical “View industry page”. Nine identical anchors waste nine links.

Part names are the page’s AEO surface. Thirty-six specific part names is what lets an assistant answer “who makes EPDM foam strips for HVAC in India?”. Which is exactly why the fourteen wrong ones matter: they are equally extractable.
Heading levels. <h2> + nine <h3> card titles inside the links. Part lists are <ul>.
Honest negatives stay in the card copy. The ISO 13485 non-claim belongs on the hub card, not only on the child page — the hub is where a medical buyer decides whether to click.
Consistency gate. These nine descriptions must not contradict the nine on the homepage sectors section or the nine child pages. Three surfaces, one source.
Images. Nine card backgrounds, loading="lazy", unique alt per card: alt="Rubber components supplied by Margo for {industry} applications".

parts.text: One card swapped. Generator & engine OEMs comes out; Specialist vehicles goes in — it is a named band in Margo’s own customer list with a real account behind it, and genset builders are not. Construction & glazing is retained and strengthened: it is the largest named sector for the extrusion and sponge/foam lines, and it is deliberately a card rather than a page until search data from those two category pages justifies promoting it.
Every card gets its own destination. Live, only the first card has a “Browse product category” link; the other five are dead cards. Six sectors, six links.
parts.lead: Every card gets its own destination.

notes: Six links recovered. Five of six cards currently link nowhere. Wiring each to its most relevant category page turns a decorative block into six contextual internal links from a Tier-1 hub.

Do not promote any of these to a page yet. A card becomes a page on a demand signal, not on ambition. Construction & glazing is the strongest candidate and the correct trigger is search data from /products/extrusion and /products/sponge-foam-rubber once the site is indexable.
Heading levels. <h2> + six <h3>.
Keep them out of the ItemList. No URL of their own, so no ListItem.
The honest framing is an asset. “These do not have a dedicated page yet” tells a buyer the site is maintained rather than padded, and it is the kind of sentence no competitor writes.
